finding.claim: update_doc calls can_edit() but discards the boolean result instead of using require_edit(), so the authorization check is a no-op. Any authenticated user can overwrite the body of any document they do not own or edit.
finding.source: Any authenticated user sending PUT /doc/<doc_id> with JSON {"body": ...} for a doc_id they have no rights to
finding.sink: doc["body"] = request.json["body"] (docs.py:20), which modifies the document content

trace.note: doc is looked up by id with no ownership scoping
can_edit(g.user, doc) returns False for the attacker but the return value is ignored, so abort(403) is never reached
body is overwritten with attacker-supplied content

finding.guards_checked: require_edit is used correctly in update_title at docs.py:27 but not here. can_edit at docs.py:7 is correct but its result is unused. No decorator or before_request auth hook exists in the file. g.user is assumed to be set elsewhere. Missing doc_id raises KeyError (500), not an access control.

verdict.guard_found: can_edit (docs.py:7-8) returns a bool, and the call at docs.py:19 is a bare statement that discards it. require_edit (docs.py:11-13) would abort(403), but it is not called in update_doc. There is no decorator or before_request hook.
verdict.reason: At docs.py:19 the bool from can_edit() is discarded, so abort(403) is never reached and docs.py:20 overwrites the body for any user who can set g.user. Every trace line matches the file, and update_title at docs.py:27 shows the correct require_edit pattern.
